summary:
Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people, and adds its own layer of measures. Law No. 17,480, sanctioned by Governor Camilo Santana and published on 19 May 2021, requires every public and private establishment in the state, effective 90 days after publication, to display a visible notice of at least 50 cm by 50 cm on the exterior or at an entrance stating that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is expressly prohibited and listing the phone number of the Special Coordination for LGBT Public Policies for complaints, clarifications and reports.

On 16 November 2006 Governor Lúcio Alcântara signed a law mandating inclusion of educational material on sexual orientation in the training of the state's Civil and Military Police, published in the Official Gazette on the 26th of that month. On 7 March 2013 State General Attorney Francisco Sales Neto issued decision 02/2013 obligating all notaries statewide to accept same-sex marriages, effective 15 March 2013; same-sex marriage has been legal in Ceará since 2013.

On 22 May 2024 the Court of Justice of Ceará authorized Brune Bonassi to rectify documents to reflect a neutral gender, making Bonassi the first non-binary person in the state to obtain such rectification. Ceará was set to issue its first birth certificate recognizing a person as non-binary. The Supreme Federal Court's 1 March 2018 ruling that a transgender person may change official name and sex without surgery or professional evaluation, by self-declaration of psychosocial identity alone, applies in the state, as does the 13 June 2019 ruling treating discrimination on grounds of gender identity and of sexual orientation as crimes akin to racism.

Violence against trans people in Ceará is documented at a high level. Per the ANTRA dossier reported by G1/Globo on 28 January 2025, Ceará was the Northeast state with the most killings of trans people in 2024, with 11 killings, the third highest raw count nationally, in a state of some 9.2 million people, about 0.12 killings per 100,000 residents. Per the 9th ANTRA dossier reported on 26 January 2026, Ceará was among the states with the most trans killings in 2025 with 8 cases, about 0.09 per 100,000 residents, tied with Minas Gerais at the top of the state ranking; Brazil totalled 80 killings, down 34% against 2024 and still the highest worldwide, with 1,261 killings recorded 2017-2025. These rankings are by raw count only and track population, so they say little about per-capita risk relative to smaller states. Among the 57 victims with race data nationally, 70% were Black, an average of 77% over 2017-2025.

On 12 December 2017 the Sobral Municipal Chamber approved Bill No. 2154/17, authored by Councillor Adauto Izidoro Arruda, prohibiting pedagogical activities reproducing the concept of "gender ideology" or any discussion of gender diversity in all municipal and private schools in Sobral, by majority vote with the sole opposing vote of Councillor Maria Socorro Brasileiro Magalhães, and forwarded the bill to Mayor Ivo Gomes to sanction or veto.
tangentialFactors:
The Supreme Federal Court's 2024 decision in ADI 5668, interpreting the National Education Plan, imposes on public and private schools nationwide a duty to combat discrimination based on gender, gender identity and sexual orientation; the Sobral bill's fate against that duty is not sourced here. In ADPF 787 the Court required the Unified Health System to guarantee trans and travesti persons full access to health services matching their physiological needs, and in precautionary decision ADPF 527 it ordered transfer of transsexual women inmates to women's prisons, followed by a National Justice Council resolution requiring a judge to set detention location after asking the detained person's preference. The Supreme Federal Court's own framing notes that Brazil leads global violence against transgender persons, with average life expectancy around 30 years against roughly 75 nationally.

Wikipedia's general overview of LGBTQ people in prison reports no codified Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, stating only that traumatic social vulnerability and stigma facing travestis and transgender people shape rehabilitation; for comparison it sets out international placement norms under which Scotland's 2022 inspection standards admit trans and intersex prisoners to facilities matching their lived or experienced gender, and Canada places prisoners by gender identity. Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil' article states that LGBTQ people have a special place in Brazilian prisons separate from other prisoners, that transgender people have the right to be called by their social name rather than their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons, and that LGBTQ prisoners may choose male or female clothing; that statement is footnoted to a Mix Brasil (UOL) article archived 18 January 2012, so its currency is unresolved.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ceará can require establishments to post the anti-discrimination notice mandated by Law No. 17,480 and route complaints through the Special Coordination for LGBT Public Policies number printed on it. State Civil and Military Police receive training that must include educational material on sexual orientation under the 2006 law. Notaries statewide have been obliged since March 2013 to accept same-sex marriages, and the Court of Justice of Ceará has granted a neutral-gender document rectification to a resident, an avenue available to others on the same reasoning.

Placement of LGBTI detainees in Ceará stands under National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021: a person is recognised as LGBTI by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing, and on arrest a judge fixes the place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, who must be told about available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and asked their preference, with the declared preference recorded, transfers prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat, LGBTI-specific living spaces barred from use as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment prohibited.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Bill No. 2154/17 in Sobral was sanctioned or vetoed by Mayor Ivo Gomes is not sourced in the inventory and remains unresolved. Whether Law No. 17,480 notices are in fact displayed across the state, and how the Special Coordination for LGBT Public Policies handles complaints, are not documented here. The enforcement record of the 2006 police-training mandate is likewise not sourced.

The 2025 ANTRA figures for Ceará are raw counts without a per-capita ranking against other states, and ANTRA's national methodology, which counts media-reported killings irrespective of motive, is contested by critics who call it unscientific and note that international comparisons are distorted by differences in documentation capacity. Whether the Court of Justice of Ceará's neutral-gender rectification has been followed by further cases is unresolved in this inventory.
